Rekha Aabhushan Cloud: Good, Better, Best

A pricing and packaging decision for a Cuttack software company serving family jewellers

1. Opening

On the evening of Friday, 2 October 2026, Rashmita Mahapatra sat in the corner office of Rekha Aabhushan Cloud in Cuttack with a printout she had already annotated twice. It carried a single question: should the company keep charging every jeweller the same ₹24,000 a year, or sell three packages at three prices? The board would meet on Friday, 9 October, and a decision was needed by then. Renewal notices for January 2027 had to go out by 20 October, so that no jeweller would face a new price in the weeks around Dhanteras, in early November, when a family shop earns a large share of its year.

Mahapatra, the founder and chief executive, knew the flat price had served the company well. She also knew that it charged a one-counter shop in Balasore the same amount as a nine-outlet family chain in Rajkot, and that only one of the two was paying for what it used.

2. Company background

Rekha Aabhushan Cloud was founded in 2016 by Mahapatra and Rajat Behera, her engineering classmate. It sells retail software to family jewellers: GST billing, karat-wise stock, old-gold exchange with melt-loss tracking, and, since the Bureau of Indian Standards made hallmarking with a HUID (hallmark unique identification) number compulsory for gold jewellery in 2023, a hallmark register that ties every piece to its HUID. The company has 3,000 paying accounts and annual recurring revenue of ₹7.20 crore, all at one flat plan. Its rivals are not other jewellery specialists so much as general tools: Tally, Zoho Books and Marg ERP, adapted with spreadsheets, and the in-house systems that large chains such as Tanishq and Kalyan run for themselves. The GST Council's 3 per cent rate on gold and the BIS rules together mean that even a tiny shop must now keep records it once did not.

The flat plan was a founder's shortcut. In 2016 nearly every customer was a single-counter shop, and one price was easy to explain. Since then the mix has changed, and success has come from the top of the base.

3. The situation

Ranjit Swain, the finance manager, built the cost-to-serve view shown in Exhibit 1 by tagging support hours, hosting and hallmark-verification calls to accounts. Emilie Tremblay, a contract data scientist in Montreal who works Indian evening hours, then joined it to a survey of 412 customers on what a year of the software was worth to them.

4. The people

Rashmita Mahapatra (chief executive, Cuttack) wants to raise revenue without breaking the trust that got the company its first 3,000 accounts. Rajat Behera (chief technology officer, Cuttack) can gate outlets and users in code within six weeks, but wants no new features built before renewals. Kishore Satpathy (head of sales, Rajkot) wants a package he can explain in one breath. Kabita Routray (customer success lead, Surat) wants the compliance features, HUID above all, left in every package, because a jeweller who cannot hallmark is a jeweller who cannot sell. Emilie Tremblay (data scientist, Montreal) wants tiers that follow measured usage, not sales instinct.

6. The options

Option A: keep one plan and raise it to ₹27,000. This is the simplest to explain and to sell. If 5 per cent of accounts leave, 2,850 remain and revenue is ₹769.50 lakh, up ₹49.50 lakh. The cost is that the counter shop still overpays, chains stay underpriced and no segment gets a package fitted to it.

Option B: three tiers, as in Exhibits 2 and 3. It yields the highest revenue, ₹877.50 lakh, and follows what each segment says it values. The cost is a harder conversation, since a jeweller in Puri will read Chain at ₹1,20,000 as a headline before reading anything else, and a switch to gating by outlets touches every account.

Option C: two tiers, Basic and Pro, split by features. Basic at ₹18,000 keeps billing and stock but withholds the HUID register; Pro at ₹48,000 includes it. Assume 1,620 Basic and 1,104 Pro accounts remain, giving ₹291.60 lakh plus ₹529.92 lakh, or ₹821.52 lakh. It is simple, yet it places a legal requirement behind a paywall, prices chains at the same level as showrooms, and hands a story to any rival or trade association that wishes to tell it.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which segment is least profitable per rupee of revenue at the flat price, and which is most exposed to a competitor?
2. Which feature in Exhibit 2 is a natural basis for a tier, and which is a compliance obligation that no tier should sell?
3. Compare the three options in revenue, accounts retained and risk to trust. What would have to be true for Option A to win?
4. What migration and communication plan would you recommend, and when should it start?

8. A note for the learner

Good, better, best packaging maps tiers to segments: each tier is the value metric, here outlets and users, bundled for the group that values it. The test is whether the price steps follow a difference the customer can see. Here they do: a one-counter shop and a nine-outlet chain have different needs, costs and stated values, which Exhibit 1 measures.

One defensible path is Option B with two changes. First, keep billing, karat stock, old-gold exchange and the HUID register in every tier, as the draft already does, because hallmarking is a legal obligation and a tier built on it would break trust with the Bureau's own rules in the background. Second, move to the new prices only at January 2027 renewals, after Dhanteras, and offer chains a two-year rate of ₹90,000 if they sign before 31 December, so that the largest accounts feel a bridge, not a cliff. Tell Satpathy's team to use one sentence per tier: one counter, two showrooms, or many outlets.

This path makes ₹877.50 lakh in the model and 56.8 per cent margin, and if the assumed 10 per cent chain churn proved too low, the extra chains lost would still be less costly than pricing every showroom and chain at today's ₹24,000. Routray should track the counter tier's churn monthly, and if it crosses 15 per cent, the company can add a ₹8,000 annual "Lite" billing plan for shops, without touching compliance.

Packaging: Good / Better / Best

The ladder is easy to draw and hard to own. This page assumes you can already build a three-tier structure around a value metric, and asks the questions that decide whether it survives contact with variable cost, an installed base, a channel, a regulator and a sales compensation plan.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On the evening of 4 March 2026, Kavya Raghunathan stayed behind in the Dhwani Speech Systems office on Bengaluru's Bannerghatta Road to reconcile two numbers that her finance team and her product team had each computed correctly and that nevertheless disagreed. Dhwani sold speech recognition and speech synthesis for eleven Indian languages as an API, mostly to contact-centre operators, bank voice bots and consumer app developers, and it had reached ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue across 2,340 paying accounts. Its packaging had been settled in 2023 and had not been touched since: a free Developer tier with 10,000 minutes, a Build tier at ₹18,000 a month, a Scale tier at ₹49,000 a month advertised as unlimited under a fair-use policy, and a negotiated Enterprise tier above that.

The number from finance was that the Scale tier ran at a 53.8% gross margin, which was low for software but not alarming for an inference-heavy product. The number from Kavya's own analyst was that the mean disguised a distribution so skewed that the average told you almost nothing true. Of the 610 accounts on Scale, the median account consumed about ₹5,150 of graphics-processor time a month against a ₹49,000 bill. The top decile — sixty-one accounts — consumed an average of ₹1,42,000 each. Nine tenths of the tier subsidised one tenth, and the subsidised tenth had grown three times faster than the rest through the December and January quarters, because word had travelled among a cluster of voice-bot agencies in Noida and Hyderabad that Dhwani's unlimited plan was the cheapest way in India to run high-volume batch transcription. Sundar Menon, Dhwani's chief financial officer, wanted blended gross margin above 70% before the Series C conversations that were scheduled to begin in July. Kavya had to decide whether to cap the Scale tier and charge overage, to abandon tiering for a platform fee plus a meter, or to keep unlimited and raise the price — and each option looked wrong in a different way to a different constituency inside the company.

Six weeks earlier and 350 kilometres south, on 19 January 2026, Ipsita Sahu had opened a conversation at Dhaatri Devices in Coimbatore that would take most of the year to close. Dhaatri had been making power-quality and energy meters for mid-size manufacturing plants since 2009 — textile units around Tiruppur, auto-component shops near Hosur, foundries in Belagavi — and had shipped its 190,000th meter in November. Hardware brought ₹210 crore in FY26 at a 47% gross margin on a list price of ₹78,000 for the flagship DH-400 panel meter. The software that read those meters, Dhaatri Insight, brought ₹31 crore, sold as a single plan at ₹1,200 per meter per month, and attached to only 38% of installed meters.

Ipsita's proposal was a four-rung ladder: a free Monitor tier bundled with every meter, a paid Analyse tier at ₹1,200, an Optimise tier at ₹3,400 that recommended load-shifting against time-of-day tariffs and scheduled captive gensets, and a Comply tier at ₹5,900 that produced evidence packs for the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Perform, Achieve and Trade cycles and for ISO 50001 audits. On a spreadsheet it roughly doubled five-year gross profit per meter shipped. It also created three problems that no spreadsheet showed. Dhaatri's 140 channel partners, who earned 22% on hardware and nothing on software, had no reason to sell it and some reason to resent it. The company's auditors would treat a free software tier bundled with a device as a second performance obligation under Ind AS 115, forcing an allocation of the device's transaction price to a service delivered over three years, which would defer roughly ₹11.5 crore of FY27 hardware revenue that Dhaatri's managing director, Ramanathan Subbiah, had already guided to. And Dana Whitfield, who ran the small North American channel from Chicago, pointed out that half her accounts had bought meters in 2019 and would now, under the new architecture, be sitting on a free tier they had already paid for.

Both decisions are packaging decisions. Neither is a decision about the number of tiers or their names. That is the first thing an expert notices: at the working-knowledge level, good/better/best is a question about how to slice a market; at the expert level, it is a question about what happens when a slicing scheme meets a cost function, a balance sheet, a channel contract and a group of human beings whose bonuses depend on the answer.

2. The idea, precisely, and the four schools that disagree about it

Define the terms carefully, because most disagreements in this area turn out to be disagreements about definitions. Packaging is the design of a menu: a finite set of offers, each a bundle of capability, capacity and service commitments, offered simultaneously to a heterogeneous population of buyers who choose among them without the seller knowing in advance which buyer is which. Good/better/best is one family of menu designs in which the offers are vertically ordered — every buyer agrees which one is better, and they differ only in how much more they will pay for it. That last clause is the whole idea. A menu of vertically ordered offers is a device for making buyers reveal, through their own choice, information about themselves that the seller cannot otherwise obtain and would be illegal or impractical to ask for.

The economics is older than software. In 1849 the French engineer Jules Dupuit described why railway companies ran third-class carriages with no roofs, and gave the explanation that still holds: the company was not saving money on roofs, it was preventing the passengers who could afford second class from travelling third. Arthur Pigou formalised the taxonomy in The Economics of Welfare in 1920, naming the practice second-degree price discrimination — discrimination by self-selection rather than by identity. The modern mathematics arrived with Michael Mussa and Sherwin Rosen's 1978 paper on monopoly and product quality and Eric Maskin and John Riley's 1984 treatment of monopoly with incomplete information, which together produced the two results that still govern the field: the highest-value segment must be left a surplus (an information rent) to stop it buying down, and the lower offer must be deliberately degraded below the level that would be efficient for its own buyers, precisely in order to shrink that rent. Raymond Deneckere and Preston McAfee gave the practice its memorable name in their 1996 paper Damaged Goods, cataloguing cases in which firms spent money to make a product worse: IBM's 1990 LaserPrinter E, mechanically identical to the LaserPrinter but fitted with chips that slowed it to five pages a minute, and Intel's 486SX, a 486DX with a working floating-point unit disabled. Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian carried the argument into information goods in Information Rules in 1998 under the label versioning, and Robert Cross's work on airline revenue management contributed the operational vocabulary of fences — the rules, such as advance purchase and Saturday-night stays, that keep a discount from leaking to buyers it was not meant for.

Running alongside this, and often confused with it, is a behavioural literature that says something different. Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto demonstrated in 1982 that adding an asymmetrically dominated option to a choice set changes the relative share of the existing options — the decoy effect. Itamar Simonson and Amos Tversky showed in 1992 that buyers exhibit extremeness aversion: a middle option gains share simply by being in the middle, regardless of its absolute merits. The economic tradition says the menu reveals a preference the buyer already had. The behavioural tradition says the menu constructs the preference. Practitioners who do not notice that these are incompatible claims tend to make an error that is easy to spot in the wild: they build a menu on economic logic and then defend it with behavioural evidence, or the reverse.

Four positions are worth stating as propositions a serious person would actually sign.

The screening school would sign: the number, content and pricing of tiers are outputs of the distribution of willingness to pay and the cost of delivering quality, not inputs; deliberate degradation of the lower tier is rational and can be welfare-improving because it lets the seller serve buyers who would otherwise be priced out entirely. It would not sign: three tiers is the right answer. Three is a convention with no standing in the mathematics; the optimal number falls out of the shape of the distribution, and for many products it is two.

The choice-architecture school would sign: the menu changes what buyers want, so the top tier earns its keep even at zero sales by making the middle tier feel moderate, and the composition of the menu is as much a communication decision as an economic one. It would not sign: each buyer has a stable reservation price that careful research can discover. Its evidence, though, is overwhelmingly drawn from individual consumers choosing in laboratory conditions, and it has never convincingly extended to a nine-person procurement committee at a bank.

The value-engineering school, the dominant school in enterprise software consulting, would sign: packaging is a product decision taken before the product is built; you research willingness to pay for each feature, sort features into leaders, fillers and killers, and assemble tiers so that each one leads with something a defined segment will pay for. It would not sign: you can repackage your way out of a product that does one job for one kind of buyer. Its weakness is that it assumes feature-level willingness to pay is measurable and additive, and in practice it is neither.

The metering school, which has gained ground since roughly 2021 and dominates in infrastructure and AI, would sign: tiers were an artefact of an era in which the marginal cost of serving one more customer was zero; where cost-to-serve is variable and material, the correct architecture is a small number of access levels plus an honest meter, and a tier ladder is at best a friendly interface on top of that meter. It would not sign: feature-gating should be the primary segmentation instrument. Its weakness is that meters are hard to forecast against, and buyers — especially Indian enterprise buyers working to annual budget approvals — reliably pay a premium for predictability.

The schools are not describing different products. They are describing the same product from four vantage points, and the expert's first move on any packaging question is to notice which vantage point the room has silently adopted.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic nobody shows you

The competent practitioner knows the procedure: find the value metric, observe the segments, draw the boundaries at natural breaks, design the middle tier to be the default, validate willingness to pay, plan the migration. The expert knows that three of those steps conceal a formal problem with a known solution, and that working it through even crudely changes the answer.

Set it up the way Kavya's team did. Let q be an index of delivered capability, where q = 1.0 is roughly what a small contact-centre operator needs. Suppose two types of buyer. Type L, small operators, are 80% of the addressable base and value each unit of q at ₹10,000 a month. Type H — large business-process outsourcers and banks — are 20% and value each unit at ₹30,000 a month. Dhwani's cost of building and serving q units to one account is ₹5,000 × q² a month, rising more than proportionally because deeper capability means more model variants, more support and more latency guarantees.

If Dhwani could see which buyer was which, it would sell each the quality at which marginal value equals marginal cost — q = 1.0 to type L at ₹10,000 and q = 3.0 to type H at ₹90,000 — and earn ₹13,000 per prospect. It cannot see. So any offer it makes to L is also available to H, and H will take it if the surplus is better. This is the incentive-compatibility constraint, and it binds.

The solution is mechanical once the geometry is clear. Let λ be the share of type L in the population. Profit is maximised by giving H the efficient quality (q = 3.0) and distorting L's quality down to qL = 1.0 − [(1 − λ)/λ] × 2.0. At λ = 0.8 that gives qL = 0.5. Price Good at exactly type L's full value for it, ₹5,000. Price Best at H's value for Best minus the rent H would earn by buying Good: ₹90,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹80,000. The gap between D and E — ₹3,000, or 23% — is what the seller pays for not knowing who is who: part information rent surrendered to type H, part output destroyed by degrading the Good tier.

Three things in that table repay attention. First, the correctly designed menu (D) beats the best single offer (A) by 11%, which is real money but is not the order-of-magnitude gain that packaging is often sold as producing; most of the real-world gain from repackaging comes from serving buyers who previously bought nothing at all, not from this mechanism. Second, architecture C — the humane menu, where the Good tier is everything a small buyer could reasonably want — earns exactly what architecture A earns, which is to say the small segment contributes nothing once the rent it forces you to pay type H is netted off. That is the damaged-goods result stated as an income statement rather than a theorem. Third, and most usefully, the formula tells you when the Good tier should not exist at all: qL goes to zero when λ falls to two-thirds. If fewer than two in three of your prospects are small buyers, the optimal Good tier is nothing.

A company whose enterprise segment is growing is a company whose entry tier is quietly becoming a liability — which is the opposite of the instinct most product teams have when growth slows.

Two further pieces of arithmetic are routinely skipped. The first is the cannibalisation breakeven. Dhwani's growth team wanted a Starter tier at ₹4,500 to catch the long tail of app developers. Farida Qureshi, who ran mid-market sales from Mumbai, estimated from her own pipeline that about 14% of the 1,180 existing Build accounts would step down. That is 165 accounts surrendering ₹13,500 each, or ₹22.3 lakh a month of gross revenue. Starter would carry roughly ₹900 of inference cost, leaving ₹3,600 of contribution. Dividing gives the breakeven: Dhwani would need 619 additional Starter accounts, a stock not a flow, merely to stand still. At the company's then-current rate of about 140 new paying accounts a month, that meant more than four months in which every single new customer went to Starter and nothing was gained. Whether that is a good trade depends entirely on whether those 619 accounts exist, which is a market-sizing question, not a pricing one — and the discipline is to notice that the packaging decision has just handed itself to a different analysis.

The second is boundary placement, and here the expert departs sharply from the competent practitioner. Everyone knows to draw boundaries at natural breaks in the data. Far fewer people look at the density of accounts around the candidate line, which is what actually determines how much pain a boundary causes. A boundary drawn through the mode of a distribution means a large population sits within a whisker of it: those accounts experience the boundary as a cliff, generate the upgrade-refusal conversations that consume sales capacity, and churn at elevated rates when they trip over it unintentionally. A boundary drawn in a trough touches few accounts and feels, to almost everyone, like it was always there.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

Good/better/best is not always right, and the conditions under which it is right can be written as claims that a team can check in an afternoon. Each is applied below to both protagonists, because the same claim can pass for one product and fail for another in the same week.

Claim 1: willingness to pay is widely and continuously dispersed. The test is the ratio of the ninetieth to the tenth percentile of realised value received — measured by usage, by outcome, or by the customer's own revenue attributable to the product. Below about three to one, the tiers will not pay for the complexity they create. Dhwani passes overwhelmingly: its ninetieth percentile account processes more than forty times the volume of its tenth. Dhaatri passes too, but for a different reason — the dispersion is not in meter count but in regulatory exposure. A 40-crore textile unit and a 900-crore designated consumer under the Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme may run the same number of meters and derive utterly different value from the same data.

Claim 2: a cheap, enforceable fence exists. The test is whether a determined buyer can reconstruct the top tier from several copies of the bottom tier. If yes, the ladder is decorative. Dhwani fails this test in its current form and knows it: three of its largest accounts run four separate Build subscriptions under different billing emails, paying ₹72,000 for what the Scale tier would have cost ₹49,000, because Build's per-minute economics were better for their pattern. That is not merely arbitrage; it is arbitrage that makes the customer worse off, which tells you the ladder is badly shaped rather than merely leaky. Dhaatri passes easily, because the fence is a physical meter with a serial number.

Claim 3: the marginal cost of serving the lowest tier is comfortably below its price. This is the claim that software took for granted for twenty years and that AI products cannot. Dhaatri's free Monitor tier costs about ₹120 per meter per month in telemetry ingestion and storage — negligible. Dhwani's proposed Starter tier costs ₹900 against a ₹4,500 price, which is fine on average and disastrous in the tail, because a single Starter account running batch jobs overnight can cost ₹30,000 in a month.

Claim 4: the buyer actually sees the menu at the moment of choice. In self-serve, the menu is a screening device and the behavioural effects are live. In enterprise, where the deal is negotiated, the published menu is an anchor and a reference frame, and self-selection barely operates: the buyer does not choose a tier, the buyer starts from the tier and negotiates away from it. Dhwani's Enterprise business behaves this way already; Dhaatri's Comply tier will, because a BEE compliance conversation happens with a plant head and a consultant in a room, not on a pricing page.

Claim 5: the complexity tax is affordable. Every tier is a permanent obligation on six systems — the entitlement service, the billing and invoicing stack, the sales compensation plan, the support severity matrix, the documentation, and the roadmap prioritisation process, which must now answer "which tier does this land in?" for every feature forever. The test is whether the organisation already has a working entitlement service. Dhwani does. Dhaatri does not: its software gating is done with a configuration flag set manually at commissioning by a field engineer, which means Ipsita's four tiers would be enforced by 140 channel partners' technicians, and the honest forecast is that they will not be.

Claim 6: the segments are stable relative to the cost of re-drawing them. Repackaging has a fixed cost measured in quarters. If the underlying distribution shifts faster than that, you are always shipping last year's ladder. Dhaatri passes: industrial energy management moves on five-year cycles. Dhwani fails, or nearly: its cost per thousand minutes of streaming recognition fell from about ₹1,050 in January 2025 to ₹310 by December after a quantisation and batching project, a 3.4-fold decline in fourteen months. A ladder whose rungs encode a cost structure that changes by a factor of three annually is a ladder that was wrong before it shipped.

Where is the idea actively misleading, rather than merely inapplicable? Three situations recur. The first is when the product does one job for one kind of buyer, and the team invents tiers anyway, splitting a coherent offer into an incoherent one and teaching every prospect to ask what they are being denied. The second is when the constraint is activation rather than monetisation — when customers who sign up do not reach value — in which case a new ladder reorganises a problem it cannot touch, and a year disappears. The third, and the subtlest, is when the apparent segments are not segments at all but stages of the same customer's life. Cross-sectional heterogeneity and longitudinal growth look identical in a snapshot. If your small customers are simply your large customers three years earlier, you do not have three segments to serve; you have one segment with an expansion path, and the right instrument is a meter that grows with them, not a ladder they must be persuaded to climb. Kavya's single most useful analytical move in February was to cohort her accounts by signup year and discover that Dhwani had both: the conversational-AI customers grew smoothly with their own businesses, while the batch-transcription customers arrived large and stayed flat. One population wanted a meter. The other wanted a plan.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

The textbook ladder assumes one product, one buyer, one seller, no regulator and no channel. Remove any of those assumptions and the practice changes.

Multi-product. Once a company sells three products, the tier ladder collides with the suite. The question becomes whether Best in product A is a rung on A's ladder or a component of the suite bundle, and the two answers imply different owners, different roadmaps and different revenue recognition. The tidy approach, which large companies describe in public, is a matrix: each product has its own ladder, and a suite bundle is assembled from a defined rung of each. What large companies actually do, once you look at the SKU table, is maintain both the matrix and a long tail of legacy combinations that no longer map to anything, because every large deal for eight years has created one. The honest treatment is to accept that SKU sprawl is not a failure of discipline but the natural sediment of enterprise selling, and to budget for periodic archaeology rather than pretending it will not accumulate.

Two-sided markets. Dhaanya Networks, a marketplace matching agri-input retailers with manufacturers across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, discovered the characteristic trap: it built a good/better/best subscription for retailers and a separate commission ladder for manufacturers, and the two ladders were designed by two teams six months apart. The result was that the retailer tier granting priority search placement destroyed the value of the manufacturer tier that had also been sold on visibility. On a two-sided platform, the tiers on each side are claims on the same scarce resource — attention, match quality, placement — and a ladder is only coherent if the total claims sold on both sides do not exceed what exists. The discipline is to model the ladder as an allocation of a fixed inventory, exactly as an advertising business does, rather than as a list of features. Very few marketplaces do this at the point of design; most discover it when the top tier on one side stops renewing.

Regulated products. Dhimahi Insure Cloud, which sells claims-processing software to insurers, learned that its customers could not repackage even when they wanted to: an insurance product variant in India is a filed product, and the IRDAI's Use and File procedure means that the equivalent of adding a Better tier is a regulatory event with a lead time, not a pricing-page change. Broadcasting offers a starker Indian example: the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's tariff orders for television constrain how channels may be bundled into bouquets, cap the discount a bouquet may offer relative to the sum of its à la carte prices, and require that every channel be separately purchasable. That is a regulator legislating directly against the packaging instrument — because the regulator's theory is that bundling in that market suppresses consumer choice rather than expressing it. The lesson for a product manager is not that regulation is an obstacle but that the boundary between legitimate versioning and coercive tying is a live contested question in several jurisdictions, and an offer that depends on a customer being unable to buy the parts separately is an offer with regulatory risk priced into it.

Consumer subscription mechanics. In India specifically, the Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework requires an additional factor of authentication for recurring card debits above ₹15,000, which is why a striking number of Indian consumer annual plans cluster just below that line. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns name thirteen practices, several of which — subscription traps, interface interference, drip pricing — describe things that a badly implemented tier ladder does by accident: a pre-selected higher plan at checkout, an upgrade that is one click and a downgrade that is a support ticket, a price that appears only after the third screen. The line between a well-designed default and a dark pattern is not a matter of intent; it is a matter of whether the cheaper option is equally reachable.

Hardware plus software. Dhaatri's case is the general one. When the software rides on hardware, four things break at once. The installed base is not yours to re-tier: meters sold in 2019 are in panels and will run for a decade. The channel that sells the hardware has no economics in the software and no mechanism to earn any. The gating is enforced in the field by people you do not employ. And the accounting changes: bundling a free software tier with a device creates a second performance obligation, and Ind AS 115 requires the transaction price to be allocated across obligations by standalone selling price. Dhaatri's auditors, valuing Monitor at a conservative ₹400 per meter per month over a 36-month expected service life, would assign ₹14,400 of standalone value to the software against ₹78,000 for the device — meaning 84.4% of each ₹78,000 collected could be recognised at delivery and ₹12,200 would be deferred over three years. At Dhaatri's shipment rate of about 9,400 meters a year, that is ₹11.5 crore of FY27 revenue moved out of the year in which it is invoiced. Nothing about the cash changes. Everything about the guided number does. This is the single most reliable way for a packaging proposal to die in a company with public or near-public reporting, and the product manager who has not spoken to the controller before the steering committee will not survive the meeting.

AI-native products. Dhwani's situation is the newest edge case and the one with the least settled practice. The classical ladder assumes the cost of the Best tier is incurred once, at build time. Inference reverses this: the cost is incurred per use, it varies by an order of magnitude across accounts within the same tier, and it falls unpredictably as models and infrastructure improve. Three consequences follow. First, gross margin can invert across the ladder — the top tier, which attracts the heaviest users and usually promises the fewest limits, can be the worst-margin tier in the business. Second, an unlimited offer is a short position on the tail of a distribution you do not control, and in AI the tail is fat because a single customer can automate a workload overnight. Third, and easily missed, falling unit costs are not straightforwardly good news for a tiered business: they compress the cost differences the ladder was built to express, and they invite competitors to reprice below you faster than your annual contracts let you follow.

What do mature companies actually do about AI cost dispersion, as opposed to what they say? Three patterns are visible in published pricing pages across 2025 and 2026. They keep the word "unlimited" and add a fair-use clause with undisclosed thresholds, enforced by a human who contacts the top fifty accounts — cheap, effective, and quietly corrosive of trust when a customer discovers the threshold by hitting it. They keep the tier ladder for access and identity and move all volume to a meter with committed-use discounts, which is honest but transfers forecasting risk to the buyer, who resists. Or they segment the model itself, routing lower tiers to smaller or quantised models, which converts a cost problem into a quality fence and is the closest modern analogue to Dupuit's roofless carriage. Each of these is a defensible answer. None of them is comfortable, which is why the practice is not settled.

6. Ten things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the entry tier is a portfolio position, not a product line, and its margin should not be read alone. The tell-tale sign is a finance review that computes contribution margin per tier and proposes killing the cheapest one. That analysis is not wrong so much as incomplete: the entry tier's return comes partly from the accounts that graduate out of it and partly from the reference frame it creates for the tiers above. But the obvious counter-reading — "never kill the entry tier, it feeds the funnel" — is equally lazy. Table 2 gives the actual condition: when the share of low-value prospects falls below roughly two-thirds, the optimal entry tier is nothing, and the correct move is to kill it. An expert holds both propositions and knows which regime the company is in; a competent practitioner holds one of them as a principle.

Two: it is almost always cheaper to add to the top than to subtract from the bottom, and the exceptions are the interesting part. The tell is an engineering estimate in which building the lower tier costs more than building the upper one, which sounds absurd until you see it — it is the signature of a team building a degradation mechanism. Deneckere and McAfee's point stands: deliberate degradation can be welfare-improving, because without it the seller serves only the high-value segment and the low-value buyers get nothing at all. But the practical asymmetry is that customers forgive a capability they never had and resent one that was removed, so degradation designed at launch is legitimate and degradation applied retroactively to an existing tier is, in the customer's experience, a price rise with extra steps.

Three: you are designing fences, not features, and the fence is whatever a determined buyer cannot easily route around. The tell is that a salesperson can name, without hesitation, three ways customers routinely get Better value on a Good plan. Seat pooling, shared API credentials, a single organisation registered as four, a partner reselling one enterprise licence across their own client base. The obvious reading is that this is an enforcement problem. It is usually a design problem: a fence that requires policing is a fence in the wrong place. The best fences are ones the customer has no wish to cross, because crossing them would also damage something the customer values — separate organisations mean separate audit trails, and a finance team that cares about audit trails will not pool them to save ₹9,000.

Four: boundaries are density decisions, not threshold decisions. The tell is a tier boundary at a round number. Round numbers are chosen by humans and natural breaks are not, so a boundary at exactly 50 seats or 100,000 API calls is prima facie evidence that nobody plotted the distribution. The subtler point, visible in Figure 2, is that the cost of a boundary is proportional to the population sitting within touching distance of it, and that population is a function of where the line falls in the density, not of how high or low it is. Two boundaries producing identical revenue in a static model can produce wildly different churn, support load and sales-cycle length.

Five: the middle tier's dominance may be evidence of extremeness aversion rather than evidence of fit, and the two have opposite implications. The tell is a natural experiment: raise the top tier's price and watch the middle tier. If middle-tier sales move and top-tier sales do not, the middle tier is being chosen relationally, not absolutely, and its price has room in it. If neither moves, the middle tier is genuinely the right product for those buyers and the menu is doing screening rather than persuasion. The reason this matters beyond satisfying curiosity is that a relationally-chosen middle tier is fragile: a competitor's differently-shaped menu changes what "middle" means, and your customers re-sort themselves without your product changing at all.

Six: every tier is a permanent tax on delivery speed, and the tax is paid by engineering, not by pricing. The tell is that the time from feature-complete to generally-available has grown, and the added time is spent in a meeting about entitlement. With three tiers, every new feature needs one decision. With three tiers, two add-ons, a legacy plan and two grandfathered cohorts, it needs a matrix, and someone has to own the matrix. This is the strongest argument the simplicity school has, and it is systematically undercounted because the cost lands in a different department from the revenue. An expert prices the tax explicitly: before adding a rung, estimate the number of entitlement decisions per quarter it creates and the engineering hours those consume, and net it against the projected revenue. It is rarely decisive, and it is occasionally decisive, which is the only reason to compute it.

Seven: under variable cost-to-serve, "unlimited" is a written option on a distribution you do not control. The tell is gross margin falling as you move up the ladder. A healthy ladder has margins that are flat or rising with tier, because the higher tier's incremental price should exceed its incremental cost. Falling margins mean the ladder is selling capacity, not capability, and has mispriced the tail. The obvious remedy — impose a cap — is right in direction and frequently wrong in execution, because a cap introduced onto an existing unlimited tier is a retroactive degradation (see nuance two) and generates exactly the reaction you would expect. The better sequencing is to introduce the metered tier alongside, price it so that the honest majority is better off on it, and let the unlimited tier become a closed legacy cohort that shrinks by attrition.

Eight: grandfathering is a balance-sheet decision wearing the costume of a kindness. The tell is a grandfathered price that appears, eighteen months later, in a competitor's proposal or in your own account executive's negotiation — because the cohort talks, and a price that exists somewhere exists everywhere. Grandfathering buys retention and buys quiet, and it sells a permanent reference price and a permanent maintenance obligation for a code path nobody wants to own. The expert practice is to grandfather with a defined, contractual expiry rather than indefinitely, to grandfather the price rather than the feature set, and to count the number of live legacy plans as a tracked metric with a target, the way one tracks technical debt.

Nine: tier mix is the leading indicator; average revenue per account is the lagging one. The tell is an ARPU line that rises while the business gets sicker, which happens routinely: a few large enterprise deals lift the average while the proportion of new customers landing on the entry tier climbs quarter after quarter, which is what a deteriorating middle looks like six months before it appears in revenue. The diagnostic an expert actually runs is a cohort-by-cohort tier-mix chart of new customers only, stripped of expansion and of the installed base, because that is the only view in which a packaging problem is visible before it is a revenue problem.

Ten: entitlement drift is real, and the pricing page is not the source of truth. The tell is a support ticket in which a customer on the Good plan reports a bug in a Better-plan feature. Over a few years, in every company of any size, the set of capabilities actually enforced in code diverges from the set described on the pricing page: features get built behind the wrong flag, a flag gets turned on for one customer and never turned off, an acquisition arrives with its own gates. The expert habit is a quarterly reconciliation — generate the entitlement matrix from the code, diff it against the published one, and treat every discrepancy as either a revenue leak or a false promise. Most companies have never run this diff. The ones that run it for the first time typically find that between five and fifteen percent of their gates are not what they think.

7. What actually differs by product type and stage, and what does not

A great deal of what is written about packaging asserts differences that do not survive scrutiny, so it is worth separating the real ones.

In consumer subscription, the real difference is that the buyer is the user and the decision is made in seconds, which makes the behavioural effects dominant and makes the number of options a first-order variable rather than a detail. Consumer packaging also runs into payment infrastructure in a way business packaging does not: the RBI e-mandate threshold shapes annual price points in India, and card decline rates shape whether an annual plan is worth more than a monthly one at the same nominal value. What is not different is the underlying screening logic; consumer ladders obey Table 1 just as enterprise ones do.

In B2B software sold to mid-market, the real difference is that the buyer is not the user, so the tier must be legible to someone who will never log in. A tier whose differentiation is a set of features is hard to justify in a budget conversation; a tier whose differentiation is a capacity, a service level or a compliance artefact is easy. This is why the most durable mid-market ladders are built on three axes at once — capability, capacity and assurance — and why Ipsita's Comply tier is likely to be Dhaatri's best seller even though it contains the least engineering.

In enterprise, the published ladder does not screen, and pretending otherwise causes real damage. Its function is to anchor, to establish a defensible list price from which discounts can be measured, and to give the account executive a structure in which to trade. The realised average selling price of a published top tier in enterprise software commonly lands between 40% and 65% of list. An expert therefore designs the enterprise rung for its negotiating properties — what can be given away cheaply, what must never be given away, what the discount ladder looks like — rather than for its self-selection properties, and treats "nobody buys the top tier at list" as by design rather than as a failure.

In platforms and marketplaces, the real difference, described above, is that tiers on both sides are competing claims on the same scarce inventory. There is a second, subtler difference: in a marketplace, a supply-side tier that improves one seller's outcomes necessarily worsens another's, so the ladder is redistributive in a way a software ladder is not, and sellers notice. Marketplaces that sell placement discover that the ladder becomes an auction whether they intended it or not.

In hardware and physical goods, the differences are almost all real and almost all unpleasant: the cost of goods puts a hard floor under the entry tier that software does not have, the installed base cannot be re-tiered, the channel must be compensated, and the accounting treatment changes. The classical price-pack architecture of consumer goods — the same shampoo in a ₹1 sachet, a ₹99 bottle and a ₹449 family pack — is genuinely good/better/best, but it discriminates on pack size and occasion rather than on capability, and the fence is the inconvenience of buying thirty sachets rather than a technical gate.

In AI-native products, the real difference is cost structure, as set out above, plus one more that is easy to miss: the quality of an AI product is stochastic, so a tier promise is a promise about a distribution. "Better accuracy on the higher tier" is a claim that must be quantified and monitored, not merely asserted, and a customer who samples ten queries and finds the cheaper tier matching the dearer one has falsified your ladder in their own mind whatever your benchmarks say.

Stage matters less than product type, but in a specific way. A company with fewer than about fifty customers does not have a distribution to analyse and should not pretend to; it should sell one or two offers, negotiate everything, and keep careful notes, because those notes are the raw material for the first real ladder. Between roughly fifty and a thousand customers, the data exists but the instrumentation usually does not, and the binding constraint is that nobody can answer "what does this account actually consume?" without a week of work. Above a few thousand customers the constraint inverts: the data is abundant and the obstacle is organisational, because by then the ladder is load-bearing for the compensation plan, the billing system and the forecast, and changing it requires the assent of people who are measured on not changing it. Dhwani, at 2,340 accounts, sat exactly at that inversion, which is why Kavya's problem was not analytical.

8. Three worked examples

Dhwani Speech Systems: unbundling the meter from the ladder

Kavya's team modelled three options against the March account base. Option one, raising Scale from ₹49,000 to ₹68,000, produced the required margin on paper and destroyed the tier: the nine deciles that were subsidising the tenth were, by definition, the accounts for whom the price was already high relative to consumption, and the churn model put losses at 22% within two quarters. Option two, capping Scale at 60,000 minutes with overage at ₹0.55 a minute, produced a cleaner margin but converted 61 of Dhwani's most engaged accounts into a hostile cohort overnight and required a public restatement of what "unlimited" had meant. Option three, which Kavya took, kept two rungs and moved volume onto a meter: Build at ₹18,000 including 20,000 minutes, Scale at ₹49,000 including 60,000 minutes, and above that a published overage rate of ₹0.55 a minute with committed-use discounts down to ₹0.34 for annual commitments above six lakh minutes. The critical design choice was that existing Scale accounts were moved onto the new structure with a twelve-month price protection rather than a cap, so the honest majority saw no change and the heavy tenth received a quote rather than a cut-off. Modelled over twelve months, blended gross margin rose from 53.8% to 71.2%; nine of the sixty-one heavy accounts declined the new terms and left, representing ₹44 lakh of annual recurring revenue and ₹1.03 crore of avoided annual inference cost. That trade — losing revenue that cost more than it brought — is the one that boards find hardest to approve and analysts find easiest to understand.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of a late catch

Tier collapse. Everyone buys the cheapest rung. The early warning is the share of new customers landing on the entry tier rising for two consecutive quarters while total new customers is flat. The diagnostic question is: what, specifically, does a buyer on the entry tier fail to accomplish? If nobody can answer in one sentence, the upper tiers have no reason to exist. Caught early this is a differentiation problem solved with one feature; caught late, after the sales team has built a year of habits around discounting the middle tier to close, it is a full repackage.

Margin inversion. Gross margin falls as you climb the ladder. The early warning is variance: the standard deviation of cost-to-serve within a tier exceeding the difference in price between tiers. The diagnostic question is: if our heaviest decile doubled tomorrow, would we make more money or less? A business that cannot answer that within an hour is not instrumented for metered pricing. Caught early, it is a cap and a meter on new customers only. Caught late, as Dhwani nearly did, it is a renegotiation with your most engaged customers at the worst possible moment.

Boundary friction. A large population sits just below a line. The early warning is a cluster in the usage histogram immediately beneath a threshold — customers managing their consumption to avoid an upgrade, which is value destroyed on both sides. The diagnostic question is: how many accounts are within 10% of a boundary, and what has their consumption growth been over six months? Flat growth in that band is the signature. Cost of a late catch is measured in the sales conversations consumed by upgrade refusals.

Fence arbitrage. Buyers reconstruct the top tier from copies of the bottom one. The early warning is multiple accounts sharing a billing domain, a payment instrument or an IP range. The diagnostic question is: what would a clever customer do to get the top tier's value for the bottom tier's price, and how long would it take them? Caught late, the arbitrage has become an expectation, and closing it reads as a price rise.

SKU sprawl and grandfather debt. The early warning is that nobody in the company can list every live plan from memory. The diagnostic question is: how many distinct price-and-entitlement combinations are we currently billing, and when does each one expire? If any answer is "never," that is the finding. The cost of a late catch is a billing migration, which is among the most expensive projects a software company can undertake and the one most likely to produce a public incident.

Compensation misalignment. Representatives sell the tier that pays them, not the tier that fits. The early warning is a divergence between the tier mix in self-serve and the tier mix in sales-assisted deals for comparable accounts. The diagnostic question is: what does a rep earn on a Good-tier deal versus a Better-tier deal, per hour of their time? If the ladder and the comp plan disagree, the comp plan wins, every quarter, without exception.

Entitlement drift. The gates in the code stop matching the gates on the page. The early warning is a support ticket about a feature the customer should not have. The diagnostic question is: can we generate the entitlement matrix from source and diff it against the pricing page today? The cost of a late catch is either an uncomfortable removal from customers who have come to rely on something, or a quiet, permanent revenue leak that no dashboard will ever surface.

Value-metric decoupling. The metric stops tracking value. The early warning is a widening scatter when realised customer outcome is plotted against billed units. The diagnostic question is: has the correlation between our value metric and our customers' own reported benefit weakened over the past year? For AI products this is the most likely failure of the next three years, because the natural metric — tokens, minutes, queries — is a measure of cost, and as the cost per unit falls it becomes a worse and worse proxy for value.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the entry tier be deliberately degraded? The screening position, steelmanned: degradation is what makes it possible to serve the low-value segment at all, because without it the rent surrendered to high-value buyers exceeds the profit the low tier generates, and the rational firm simply abandons the small customer. The evidence is the mathematics of Table 1 and a long empirical record from railways to printers to processors. The opposing position, steelmanned: in a market with switching costs and word of mouth, a deliberately crippled entry product creates a population of disappointed users who are a permanent drag on brand and referral, and the model's assumption that buyers' valuations are exogenous is exactly wrong for products people talk about. This position would be falsified if a firm that shipped an honestly good entry tier could be shown, over several years, to earn less than a comparable firm that degraded — and the studies that would settle this do not exist, because no firm runs the experiment at a scale and duration that would resolve it.

Three tiers, or two plus a meter? The traditional position rests on the observation that buyers, especially committee buyers, pay a real premium for a predictable annual number, and that a meter transfers forecasting risk to the party least able to bear it. The evidence is the persistence of committed-use contracts even in cloud infrastructure, where metering is technically trivial: buyers repeatedly choose to pre-commit at a discount rather than pay as they go. The metering position rests on the observation that fixed tiers under variable cost are a wager, that the wager is losing more often as workloads become automated, and that every fixed-price AI product of 2024 and 2025 that promised unlimited usage has since capped, metered or repriced. It would be falsified if inference costs fell far enough and fast enough that cost-to-serve became negligible again, which is not impossible, and which would make this entire argument a footnote about a five-year anomaly.

Does the compromise effect survive in B2B? The behavioural position holds that a middle option gains share by virtue of position, and that this is among the most replicated findings in consumer choice. The sceptical position notes that essentially all of the evidence comes from individuals choosing in single-shot laboratory tasks, that enterprise purchases involve committees, written justifications, procurement rules and repeat play, and that no well-identified field study has demonstrated extremeness aversion in a purchase above roughly ten lakh rupees. The sceptics would be wrong if a large-scale field experiment varying the top tier's price across matched enterprise segments moved middle-tier share; such an experiment is straightforward to run and almost nobody runs it, because pricing changes are rarely randomised.

How often should packaging change? The continuous-optimisation position treats packaging as a product surface to be iterated, and points out that a ladder built on last year's cost structure is simply wrong. The stability position holds that a price is a promise, that buyers make multi-year plans against it, and that a vendor who reprices annually teaches its customers to treat it as a commodity supplier and to negotiate accordingly. The evidence for stability is that the software companies with the highest net retention tend to have the most boring pricing histories. The evidence for iteration is that the companies growing fastest in AI have repriced two or three times in eighteen months. It is possible both are true and the variable is market maturity, but nobody has shown it.

Is packaging a product decision or a marketing decision? This is the disagreement that determines who owns the roadmap, and it is fought in most companies without being named. The product position: the tier boundary determines what gets built, because a feature's tier assignment decides its funding, so packaging is upstream of the roadmap and must be owned by product. The marketing position: the tier boundary is a communication artefact that must be legible to a market, and product teams consistently build ladders that are internally coherent and externally unintelligible. Both are correct about the other's failure mode, which is why the argument does not resolve and why the companies that handle it best tend to be the ones that make the ownership explicit rather than the ones that pick the theoretically correct owner.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied packaging produces a three-tier slide with a highlighted middle column. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways.

They ask about the distribution before they ask about the segments, because the shape of the density determines both the number of tiers and where the lines can go, and no amount of qualitative segmentation research substitutes for a histogram. They compute the cannibalisation breakeven before proposing a lower tier, and they state it as a number of accounts rather than as a percentage, because a number of accounts can be argued with. They go to the controller before the steering committee, because in any company with an audit, revenue recognition can kill a packaging proposal and nobody in product will see it coming. They read the compensation plan as part of the packaging design, on the understanding that a ladder the sales organisation is not paid to climb is a ladder nobody climbs. They design the migration at the same time as the structure, and they write down which cohort is grandfathered, for how long, and what happens on the day it ends, because an undated concession is a permanent one. And they hold the tension between the schools rather than resolving it: they will use the screening mathematics to size the entry tier and the behavioural evidence to position the middle one, and they will say out loud which claim they are relying on for which decision, so that when the ladder underperforms, the team knows which assumption to test.

One more habit distinguishes them, and it is the least glamorous. They look at the ladder they inherited before they design the one they want, and they reconstruct why each rung exists — which quarter it was added in, which deal forced it, which executive sponsored it. Most bad ladders are not bad designs; they are good designs from four years ago with three years of exceptions welded on. Knowing which is which is most of the work.

12. What Kavya and Ipsita decided

Kavya Raghunathan presented on 27 March 2026 and got approval for the two-rung-plus-meter structure described above, with three conditions she had proposed herself. The first was that the migration would run new-customer-first, with the existing Scale cohort left untouched for two full quarters while the new structure's behaviour was observed. The second was that the sixty-one heavy accounts would be contacted individually by Farida's team with a commercial proposal before any published change, on the principle that the customers who would be most affected should not learn about it from a blog post. The third, which Sundar Menon resisted and then accepted, was that Dhwani would publish its overage rate rather than negotiate it, because Kavya's argument — that a hidden rate in a market where costs were falling would be read as opportunism and would cost more in trust than it earned in margin — was the one argument in the room that nobody could rebut. She was candid that the structure would need revisiting inside eighteen months; the cost curve she was pricing against had moved by a factor of three in the previous fourteen.

Ipsita Sahu's ladder shipped in a reduced form on 1 April 2027, the start of FY28, fifteen months after she first proposed it. Monitor remained free but was rebranded as an included feature of the device rather than a tier, on the controller's advice, to simplify the standalone-selling-price argument. Analyse and Optimise launched as planned. Comply was deferred and then launched separately in September 2027 as a service engagement with software attached rather than a software tier, because the finding from thirty customer conversations was that plants buying BEE compliance support were buying a consultant's signature, not a dashboard, and the packaging had to match what was actually being bought. Partners received their 15% recurring referral commission and, in the first two quarters, originated 44% of paid software attaches — below Ipsita's forecast and far above the zero they had originated before. The pre-2024 installed base kept Analyse free for life, and Ipsita stopped describing that as a concession and started describing it as the cost of the company's earlier promise, which was more accurate and, she found, ended the argument.

Discussion questions

1. Table 2 shows that as the high-value segment grows, the optimal entry tier shrinks to nothing. Dhwani's batch-transcription customers were exactly such a segment, and they were growing three times faster than the rest. On that evidence, should Kavya have removed the Build tier rather than adding a meter to Scale? What does the model not capture that would justify keeping it?

2. Dhaatri's packaging was altered by the controller, the channel director and the North American channel head before it reached a customer, and each alteration was individually defensible. At what point does a packaging design that has been negotiated internally stop being a design at all? How would you know, from inside the company, that the line had been crossed?

3. Dhyana Learning's five-plan structure produced a 3.6% ARPU gain and a 22% conversion loss, and the ARPU gain was the number reported monthly. Design the single metric you would have put on the growth team's dashboard in January 2025 that would have surfaced the damage within six weeks — and say what that metric would have made harder to see.

13. Going deeper

The value metric
The rung spacing in every ladder above is really a statement about a single underlying unit; get the unit wrong and no amount of tier design recovers it. Revisit it whenever a boundary starts generating arguments.
Freemium vs free trial
Determines what sits below the Good tier and why. Dhaatri's free Monitor tier is freemium with an accounting consequence; a trial would have had none.
What pricing signals
Tier names and price points are read as quality claims before they are read as costs; the gap between what a ladder means and what it says is where most positioning damage occurs.
Enterprise pricing and negotiation
Explains why the published top rung behaves as an anchor rather than an offer, and what the 40–65% realised-to-list ratio is actually made of.
Bundling and unbundling
The horizontal counterpart to this vertical ladder: what to combine across products, when regulators object, and why the same mechanism looks like value creation in one market and tying in another.
Price-pack architecture for goods
The consumer-goods version of the same discipline, discriminating on pack size and occasion; the sachet-to-family-pack ladder is the purest good/better/best in Indian retail.
Repackaging and tier migration
The half of the job that Dhyana Learning got wrong and Dhwani got right — grandfathering, cohorts, legacy SKUs, and the day the concession expires.
When to charge
Timing interacts with the ladder: a rung introduced before a segment exists creates a category of confused buyers, and one introduced after a competitor's is a response rather than a design.
Willingness-to-pay research
Supplies the distribution that Figure 1 and Table 1 assume you already have; without it the screening mathematics is a well-shaped guess.
AI cost-to-serve and pricing
The direct sequel to Figure 3: how to price when the tenth decile costs thirty times the median and the unit cost falls by a third every two quarters.
Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing
Sets the level once the structure is fixed; a correct ladder priced from cost is the most common way a good packaging project produces a mediocre result.
Discounting and promotions
Every discount is a temporary, unlabelled new tier; a company that discounts habitually has more rungs than it thinks and none of them documented.
Raising prices
The instrument of last resort and first temptation. Kavya rejected it in favour of restructuring; understanding when that is the right call, and when it is avoidance, is the natural next study.

Part of a product-management knowledge graph module on Go-to-Market, Growth and Monetisation. This page assumes the working-knowledge treatment of packaging — segments, value metrics, tier boundaries and the basic migration plan — and takes up what happens when that structure meets variable cost, an installed base, a channel, a regulator and a compensation plan. Companies, individuals and figures in this page are illustrative; regulators, standards and named academic work are real.

Fehrist Channel Systems: The Price Card Nobody Can Defend

Jorhat, November 2026 — repackaging a distributor management system when the brand pays and the distributor uses

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 15 November 2026, the first floor above a tyre and battery shop on A.T. Road in Jorhat held Lakhimi Hazarika, vice-president of product at Fehrist Channel Systems, and three versions of the same price card. Diwali had ended the week before, and the loading season with it. On Friday she would take one to the board; it had to reach customers by 1 December, because every principal-funded contract signed since 2019 required a hundred and twenty days' notice and the card took effect on 1 April 2027.

Fehrist sold Lehraav, a distributor management system for secondary-sales capture, scheme settlement, van-sales beats and returns. Annual recurring revenue was ₹36.90 crore. At full realisation the card lifted that by ₹459.60 lakh a year, a rise of 12.5 per cent — not, she had written, the thing worth arguing about. Underneath sat some ₹110 crore of three-year revenue whose price and timing turned on how the installed base moved across.

Three further notes sat in that margin. She could not say how many accounts the company had. Two willingness-to-pay studies on her desk, both properly run, ranked the same six features in almost opposite order. And whoever most wanted the feature at the top of the card was not whoever would pay for it.

2. How the company got here

Zubeen Sonowal founded Fehrist in 2014 out of a family tea-trading business. His first customer was a stockist three streets away who kept godown stock in a hardbound register. Lehraav grew out of that register, and by 2018 reached two thousand distributors across Assam, Tripura and north Bengal.

The decision that shaped everything came in 2019. Yaadein Consumer Care, a personal-care principal with its plant at Meerut and its eastern office at Agra, offered to pay for Lehraav licences on behalf of its own distributors, so that it could see retailer-level secondary sales rather than monthly summaries. Sonowal signed. Principal Assist brought volume, western Uttar Pradesh and a second class of paying customer. It also brought the hundred-and-twenty-day notice and a most-favoured-rate clause: no distributor in a principal's network could be charged less than the principal paid for a comparable licence. In September 2026 counsel in Silchar concluded that the clause reached distributor pricing too, so any introductory discount cascaded into every funded contract in that network.

In March 2021 Fehrist published its first real card: Godown at ₹36,000 and Territory at ₹1,08,000, both per billed login per year. Nobody thought the billing unit a decision. It was what the system could count.

3. The industry

India's packaged-goods trade still reaches most of its retail through independent distributors and stockists: several lakh family firms. Principals such as Dabur, Marico, Britannia, Tata Consumer Products and Amul have spent a decade trying to see past the primary invoice into what the retailer actually bought, and the software promising that visibility is crowded — Bizom, FieldAssist, Botree, SAP, Zoho. GST, e-invoicing and UPI collections on NPCI's rails made the data cleaner, the compliance heavier and the distributor's patience with slow software shorter, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 raised a question the channel had never asked: when a distributor's system reports a named kirana store's purchases to a brand, whose data is that.

Reliance Retail's direct-to-retailer programmes and quick commerce, Zepto and Blinkit among them, were pulling volume off the classical beat, making distributors price-sensitive as principals grew keener to pay for visibility. A multinational home-care principal also ran a three-state pilot from its category team in Ho Chi Minh City, where Tran Bao Linh wanted the same reporting across South-East Asia in 2028, on one contract, one rate, one package.

Packaging: Good / Better / Best

Which tiers map to which segments — and why the ladder you build determines who buys, who upgrades, and who quietly leaves.

1. A ladder with only one rung

On the morning of 11 February 2025, Arjun Deshmukh opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding for three weeks. Arjun was VP of Product at Tarnika Systems, a Pune-based company that sold warehouse and fulfilment software to Indian D2C brands, kirana aggregators, and regional third-party logistics operators. Tarnika had just crossed 1,400 paying customers and ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue, and on paper the business looked healthy. Underneath, it was not. Growth had slowed from 40% year-on-year to 14%, and the board had asked a question Arjun could not yet answer with numbers: why did a customer running one warehouse in Nashik pay the same ₹15,000 a month as a customer running eleven warehouses across four states?

Tarnika sold a single plan. Every customer, regardless of size, got the same dashboard, the same number of user seats, the same API limits, and the same ₹15,000 monthly fee. It had been an easy plan to sell in 2021, when the company had eleven customers and Arjun's predecessor wanted to remove pricing as an objection. By 2025 it was actively hurting the business in two directions at once. A one-warehouse D2C seller in Indore, doing perhaps ₹40 lakh a month in shipped goods, found ₹15,000 painful relative to the value received and churned within four months more often than not. A forty-two-warehouse 3PL chain headquartered in Ahmedabad, meanwhile, was extracting enormous value from Tarnika's route-optimisation and multi-location inventory sync — value it would have paid five times as much for — and was capped at the same ₹15,000, with an account manager privately warning Arjun that if a competitor priced it correctly, Tarnika would lose that account before the next renewal. The company had, in other words, a packaging problem masquerading as a growth problem: one price could not simultaneously serve two very different jobs the product was doing for two very different customers. Arjun had six weeks before the March board meeting to bring a redesigned structure, and the Series C term sheet on the table had a pricing-diligence clause attached to it.

2. The idea, stated plainly

Packaging is the decision of how many distinct offers to sell, what each one contains, and which customer segment each one is built for — as opposed to pricing, which is the separate decision of what number to charge for each offer once it exists. The most common packaging architecture in software and many services businesses is good / better / best (GBB): three (occasionally four) named tiers, ordered by the amount of value delivered, each built around a chosen value metric — the unit that scales with the value a customer gets, such as warehouse locations, seats, API calls, or shipment volume — so that a customer's usage naturally sorts them toward the tier suited to them. The practice of anchoring a purchase decision with three deliberately ordered options is old: catalogue retailers were doing it a century ago, and the psychologist Dan Ariely's well-known 2008 experiment with Economist magazine subscriptions showed how the presence of a deliberately unattractive middle option could shift buyers toward the option a seller most wanted sold. Its modern codification for subscription software is younger and is closely associated with pricing consultancies such as Simon-Kucher and with practitioners like Madhavan Ramanujam, who argued in his 2016 book Monetizing Innovation that most companies leave money on the table not because their price is wrong but because they sell one thing to everyone instead of several things to the people who actually want each one.

Packaging exists to solve a specific problem: a single product, sold at a single price, cannot capture the different amounts different segments are willing to pay for it, and cannot avoid either overcharging price-sensitive small customers into churn or underpricing high-value customers into someone else's arms — precisely the trap Tarnika had fallen into. The sentence Arjun could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: packaging turns one price into a ladder of value, so each segment self-selects the rung that matches what it needs and what it will pay, without Tarnika having to guess on a customer's behalf.

3. How the ladder actually gets built

Constructing a good/better/best structure is not a naming exercise; it is a sequence of analytical steps, several of which practitioners routinely skip and later regret. The first step is to identify real segments in the existing customer base — not assumed segments, observed ones. Arjun's team pulled usage logs for all 1,400 accounts and found that the single most predictive variable for both usage intensity and willingness to pay was not company size in employees or revenue, but the number of physical warehouse locations a customer operated inside Tarnika. That became the candidate value metric: the dial that would move price up and down as a customer's own value from the product grew.

The second step is to separate what each segment actually uses from what it merely tolerates having bundled in. Tarnika's smallest customers, it turned out, never touched the multi-location inventory sync feature and used barely a third of the API call allowance baked into the flat plan — they were paying for capability they did not need. Its largest customers were hitting API ceilings weekly and manually requesting workarounds from support, a clear signal of unmet, unpriced demand. The third step is to draft tier boundaries around the value metric, choosing break points that fall at natural discontinuities in the data rather than round numbers chosen for tidiness. The fourth step, frequently skipped, is to design the middle tier deliberately as the one most customers should rationally choose — because a well-built "Growth" or "Business" tier both anchors the top tier as reasonable by comparison and captures the bulk of the addressable market, while an under-designed one leaves customers guessing and defaulting to the cheapest option. The fifth step is to validate the proposed structure against real willingness-to-pay data — through van Westendorp price-sensitivity surveys, structured win/loss interviews, or, as Arjun chose, a controlled analysis of actual usage-to-revenue ratios across existing accounts — before committing to it. The sixth and last step, and the one Arjun's team had underestimated going in, is planning the migration: deciding how existing customers move from the old single plan onto the new ladder without a support and churn spike large enough to erase the very revenue gain the redesign was meant to produce.
