5. The nuances a learner has to sit with

Packaging is not pricing, and conflating them hides the real lever. A team that argues about whether Growth should cost ₹22,000 or ₹25,000 while leaving the tier boundaries and feature list untouched is optimising the wrong variable first. Get the segmentation and the value metric right before arguing over the number; a correct structure at a mediocre price outperforms a correct price on a broken structure almost every time, because the structure decides who even considers buying.

Anchoring works, but it has an honesty limit. Ariely's Economist experiment showed that a deliberately unattractive middle option can push buyers toward a more expensive one; Tarnika's Growth tier used a milder, defensible version of the same principle by making it visibly the best value per location rather than by making Starter or Enterprise artificially bad. The line between skilful anchoring and manipulative decoy pricing is whether every tier, examined on its own, is still a fair deal — regulators and customers both eventually notice when it is not.

Tiers should map to jobs, not to company size. Two customers with identical revenue can have wildly different needs from the same software; Tarnika's early instinct to segment by company turnover would have misclassified several fast-growing single-warehouse D2C brands as "small" when their real behaviour — heavy API usage, frequent support contact — belonged in Growth. The value metric has to track actual usage of what the product does, not a proxy for size that merely correlates with it some of the time.

Feature-gating and usage-based gating solve different problems and are often combined. Feature-gating (withholding a capability, like multi-location sync, from lower tiers) segments by need; usage-based gating (capping API calls or seats, then charging overage) segments by volume within a need that is already met. Most mature SaaS ladders, Tarnika's included, blend both: a feature unlocks at Growth, and a usage cap on top of that feature scales further within Enterprise.

Migrating existing customers is a project of its own, not an afterthought. A repackaging that improves new-customer economics but mishandles the installed base can lose more in surprise churn and support cost than it gains in higher average revenue. Grandfathering some cohort of existing customers on their old price for a defined window, and communicating the change well before the bill changes, is not generosity — it is risk management.

Packaging cannot tell you what to charge, only how to structure the offer. Even a flawless three-tier ladder built around the right value metric leaves the actual price points to be set by separate willingness-to-pay research; a beautifully structured ladder priced by guesswork is still guesswork, just organised guesswork.

The middle-tier trap is real and easy to fall into by accident. If Growth is priced too generously relative to Enterprise, large customers will simply buy several Growth accounts, or stay on Growth and quietly exceed its intended usage, rather than upgrade — Tarnika found early evidence of exactly this in accounts running 18–19 locations who had never been asked to move up, a sign the boundary and the enforcement of it, not just the price, needed attention.

A newcomer should ask what happens at the edges of each tier before trusting the structure. What does a customer sitting one unit below a boundary actually experience — friction, a clean upgrade prompt, or nothing at all? A ladder that has clear rungs on a slide but no mechanism nudging customers between them in the live product is a plan, not yet a working system.

6. How the ladder changes by product type and company stage

In consumer subscription products — Spotify's Free, Individual, Duo, and Family tiers are the standard teaching example — packaging tends to rely more heavily on feature and household-size gating than on usage metering, because consumer buyers respond poorly to being billed by the unit and prefer flat, predictable tiers; testing is cheap and fast, since a consumer app can A/B test a new tier structure on a slice of new signups within days. In B2B software like Tarnika's, packaging usually pairs a self-serve ladder for smaller segments with a sales-assisted, negotiated top tier for the largest accounts, because enterprise buyers expect customisation, procurement cycles, and a named account manager that a self-serve price page cannot provide — which is exactly why Tarnika's Enterprise row in Table 1 shows an average price rather than a fixed one. In marketplace products, packaging frequently has to be built twice, once for each side: a ride-hailing or quick-commerce platform might package subscription perks for demand-side customers while packaging commission tiers and priority-placement bundles quite differently for its supply-side sellers or riders, and the two ladders can pull against each other if not designed jointly.

Stage matters as much as product category. An early-stage company with thirty customers rarely has the usage data to build a defensible value metric and typically runs one or two hand-negotiated plans, effectively doing packaging manually, deal by deal, the way Tarnika itself did in 2021. A company at Tarnika's stage, with over a thousand customers, has enough data to detect real segments statistically but often still lacks a dedicated pricing function, which is why the redesign fell to Arjun's product team rather than to a specialist. Large, mature companies — the Freshworks and Zoho scale of Indian SaaS — typically run formal, quarterly packaging reviews, dedicated pricing analysts, and far more granular usage-based add-ons layered on top of a simpler base ladder, because at that scale even small percentage shifts in tier mix move real money.

7. Common mistakes worth watching for

Gating features by guesswork instead of usage data. The symptom is a middle tier with unusually high churn shortly after signup, because customers bought it expecting a capability that turned out to live in the tier above or below. The underlying error is assuming what a segment values instead of measuring what it actually touches in the product. The cheapest diagnostic is a simple feature-adoption funnel run against each tier before finalising the gate list, which is precisely what caught Tarnika's over-provisioned Starter plan.

Building too many tiers. The symptom is a lengthening sales cycle and prospects who ask, unprompted, "which one am I supposed to pick?" The underlying error is trying to solve every edge case with a new named plan instead of accepting that a handful of usage-based add-ons can flex a smaller number of tiers further than a fifth or sixth tier ever will. The cheap diagnostic is tracking win rate and time-to-close by tier; both degrade visibly once a ladder passes four rungs.

Packaging around company size rather than the value metric. The symptom is customers who are clearly outgrowing or underusing their tier relative to peers of similar revenue. The underlying error, as above, is treating a correlate of value as the value metric itself. The cheap diagnostic is plotting actual usage against current tier for a sample of accounts and looking for a wide scatter rather than a clean line.

Skipping the migration plan. The symptom is a spike in support tickets and cancellations in the weeks after a repackaging launch, arriving faster than any genuine dissatisfaction with the new tiers could explain. The underlying error is treating packaging as a pricing-page change rather than a change-management exercise for an existing customer base. The cheap diagnostic is running the new packaging past a canary segment of existing customers first and watching their reaction before a full rollout — the step Arjun insisted on adding to his own six-week timeline after seeing this mistake documented in a peer company's public post-mortem.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well: a product team identifies a value metric that genuinely tracks the value customers receive, validates it against real usage data across hundreds of accounts rather than a handful of anecdotes, draws tier boundaries at the natural breaks in that data rather than round numbers, builds a middle tier deliberately designed to be the sensible default, prices each tier only after separate willingness-to-pay research rather than intuition, and ships the new ladder to new customers first while giving the existing base a defined, communicated grandfathering window before anyone's bill changes. Nothing about this is exotic; the discipline lies entirely in doing the steps in order and not skipping the ones that feel like paperwork, which is exactly where Tarnika's original single-plan design had failed six years earlier.

9. What Arjun decided, and what comes next

Arjun brought the board a three-tier structure — Starter, Growth, and Enterprise — built on warehouse-location count as the value metric, with the Growth-to-Enterprise boundary moved to 15 locations rather than 20, a sales-assisted process for any account above that line, and a twelve-month grandfathering window for existing customers before their price changed. He did not promise the board an immediate revenue jump; he showed them the retention-adjusted math from Table 1 and argued that the redesign traded a short-term dip for a structurally healthier base — lower churn among small accounts, and a pricing ceiling on large accounts that no longer sat needlessly below what those customers were plainly willing to pay. The board approved it, with the migration plan as an explicit condition.

What Arjun's team needed to learn next followed directly from this decision. Having built the ladder, the next open question was how far down that ladder to let anyone in for free — the freemium-versus-free-trial choice governs how a Starter tier actually acquires its first customers, and Tarnika had not yet decided. Close behind it sat the harder question of how the Enterprise rung, sold by negotiation rather than self-serve, should actually be priced and structured deal by deal — the subject of enterprise pricing and negotiation, which the Table 1 "average price" line had quietly deferred rather than answered.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. If a customer's usage puts them right at a tier boundary but they show no sign of wanting to upgrade, is that a pricing failure, a product failure, or simply a customer who is correctly sized for exactly what they need?

2. Tarnika chose warehouse locations as its value metric because it was the best available proxy for value in 2025 — what would have to change in the business for that proxy to stop being the right one, and how would the team notice in time?
